title: HPACK-06: define the semantics of header_table_size in terms of SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE
body:
Currently, header_table_size is defined as:

```
header table size adjusted before encoding/decoding the header set.
```

I suggest that we should define header_table_size in terms of reception and transmission of SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE. For encoder, header_table_size means that the same value was received from the remote peer just before the encoding the current header set. For decoder side, header_table_size means that it sent its value in SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE and ACK was received from the peer before decoding. If SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE was not received/transmitted since the previous encoding/decoding, header_table_size key must be omitted.

The omitting header_table_size is very important for HPACK-06. In HPACK-05, presence of the same value of header_table_size in sequence does not affect the encoding or decoding since the header table size is solely announced by decoder and changing to the same header table size is just like noop.

In HPACK-06, things have changed. HPACK-06 introduced the ability for the encoder to declare its selected table size encoded in header block after SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE was received. For example, the decoder sends 8192 as SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE. If encoder wants to use 4096, then it encodes the value as described in the spec. The important thing is that this value, 4096, is effective just before the encoder receives the SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE from the decoder again. If encoder receives the 2nd SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE, 8192, then encoder has to emit 4096 again, because without this emission, the header table size would be 8192. For this reason, repeatedly setting header_table_size with the same value has to be made when you know what you are doing.

title: HPACK-06: Remove "context" key
body: In HPACK-05, context key was important because we needed it to switch Huffman code table. But HPACK-06 unifies Huffman code table for both request and response, which means we no longer have to care about whether the input is request or response. This means that we don't need "context" any more. For this reason, I suggest that remove "context" from the specification of our format.

title: headers
body:
The format of `headers` is strange to me:

``` json
      "headers": [
        [ ":method", "GET" ],
        [ ":scheme", "http" ],
        [ ":authority", "example.com" ],
        [ ":path", "/" ]
      ]
```

It's OK to use the outer array to keep the order. But why inner arrays are used? It should be a singleton object:

``` json
      "headers": [
        {":method": "GET"},
        {":scheme": "http"},
        {":authority": "example.com"},
        {":path": "/"}
      ]
```
